audits.title: Behavioural statistics for a maze-solving agent
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive statistical analysis confirming most distance effects; it holds one brief failed sub-result, a second-batch non-replication of one distance effect.
experiments: Second-batch check of the Euclidean cheese-to-decision-square distance effect
Single-variable screen where five of eleven distance variables failed to beat the baseline
Decision-square-to-top-right 5x5 distance effect from the earlier post, dismissed as an artifact
audits.primary_experiment: Second-batch check of the Euclidean cheese-to-decision-square distance effect

hypothesis.evidence: Authors expected both spatial and legal-step closeness between decision square and cheese to raise cheese-getting; spatial effect held only at low confidence.

claim_scope.evidence: Single agent; 10,000 runs, 5,239 levels with a decision square, logistic regressions with 80/20 splits, then a second independent 10,000-run batch.

method.evidence: Logistic regression per variable, L1-regularized multiple regression, variable-dropping accuracy comparisons, variance inflation factors, manual maze edits.

models.evidence: Agent is only described as the maze-solving policy network from earlier work; no model name or architecture appears in the post.

result_direction.evidence: Effect seen in the first batch but absent in a second independent batch, while other results reproduced.

failure_type.evidence: Authors only suspect the effect would be clearer with action-logit statistics rather than cheese-getting frequencies; not tested because of overhead.

quote.value: we found no loss at all when dropping this variable from 1)-3)
quote.evidence: Reports that a second independent batch showed zero accuracy cost from removing that variable.

audits.notes: Mostly a positive analysis; the negative result is one sentence plus a footnote; second-batch numbers are not given.

audits.title: Fuzzing LLMs sometimes makes them reveal their secrets
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive elicitation write-up; the password-locked model and noisy-exploration RL experiments gave little or no benefit and are described in detail.
experiments: Random noise on a password-locked math model to unlock sandbagged answers
Noise-augmented expert iteration for RL exploration on the same password-locked model
audits.primary_experiment: Random noise on a password-locked math model to unlock sandbagged answers

hypothesis.evidence: States a hope that added noise can surface hidden or sandbagged behavior; cites earlier weight-noise work that partly unlocked password-locked models.

claim_scope.evidence: 32 random MATH test problems, random noise only, best of 100 vectors, temperatures 0 and 1; post lists many untried noise variants.

method.evidence: Adding random noise to activations, choosing the best of 100 noise vectors; also noisy sampling inside an expert-iteration RL loop.

models.evidence: Password-locked model is identified only by its source paper title; Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct is named only for the other, positive experiments.

result_direction.evidence: Noise barely helped at temperature 1 and not at all at temperature 0, weaker than the Qwen runs and earlier weight-noise work.

failure_type.evidence: Author suspects improved search methods could help far more and lists untried options: more noise vectors, other noise placements, smarter noise tuning.

quote.value: only a small uplift at temperature 1, and no uplift at temperature 0
quote.evidence: Says noise gave the locked model a slight gain at the higher sampling temperature and no gain at the lower one.

audits.notes: Mostly a positive elicitation post; failure numbers are in plots, not text; one subsection plus the RL attempt.

audits.title: Models don’t seem to be dishonest in the way humans are
audits.genuine_reason: The post reports fine-tuning on true versus false model-written reasoning and finding no differential effect on dishonesty evals; stronger variants gave only weak transfer.
experiments: Training on own true versus false gender-inference reasoning (filter and overwrite arms), tested on dishonesty evals
Off-policy reveal versus rephrase targets
GRPO and DPO variants of the training setup
Persuasive-but-false subset confirmed by a belief probe
Deceptive versus neutral framing in the prompt
audits.primary_experiment: Training on own true versus false gender-inference reasoning (filter and overwrite arms), tested on dishonesty evals

hypothesis.evidence: Poses a fork between human-like dishonesty and arbitrary faulty mapping and asks which training teaches; no stated expectation for the true-versus-false comparison.

claim_scope.evidence: Qwen 2.5 32B, 400 blog posts (284 correct), gender inference only; transfer tested on a 90-question censorship set and others; Gemma 3 27B replicates.

method.evidence: Filter and overwrite arm constructions, Claude-judge scoring and a linear belief probe are named; GRPO and DPO appear as variant runs; base recipe left unspecified.

models.evidence: Qwen 2.5 32B and Gemma 3 27B trained; Claude used as judge and answer rephraser.

result_direction.evidence: Deception-related censorship scores matched between false and true arms; both shifted from baseline equally, so the training itself explains the change.

failure_type.evidence: Authors conclude wrong-answer targets by themselves do not teach broad deception, though they also name a narrow, short-horizon training setup as a possible cause.

quote.value: True and false training usually produced nearly identical downstream effects
quote.evidence: Summary line saying the two arms, trained on correct versus incorrect labels, led to almost the same downstream behavior.

audits.notes: Several results are in figures missing from the text; training hyperparameters and number of steps are not given.

audits.title: Do capabilities generalize across propensities?
audits.genuine_reason: Descriptive intermediate results, mostly showing full transfer on simple tasks; the negative pieces are low transfer on Chess and reasoning, and propensity adherence collapsing.
experiments: Chess puzzles with bold/plain and hedging/confident propensity swaps (gpt-oss-120b): large performance gap
Reasoning versus no-reasoning swap: reduced transfer on post-cutoff facts
Propensity adherence collapse under swapped prompts
Pre-training named personas before main training, with no improvement
audits.primary_experiment: Chess puzzles with bold/plain and hedging/confident propensity swaps (gpt-oss-120b): large performance gap

hypothesis.evidence: Background calls bold formatting cosmetic with no bearing on problem-solving; hedging/confident gets only a descriptive line, so the stated expectation covers bold/plain alone.

claim_scope.evidence: Lichess puzzles, gpt-oss-120b, SFT, toy tasks, no RL; adherence loss limits bold/plain Chess results to about 1000 steps; puzzle count not given.

method.evidence: Supervised fine-tuning on paired tasks with opposite propensities, evaluation under swapped propensity prompts, performance-gap and adherence metrics, Claude Sonnet-generated training completions.

models.evidence: gpt-oss-120b for the Chess figure; Llama 3.1-8B in the appendix; Claude Sonnet generates training completions.

result_direction.evidence: For the formatting and hedging pairs, swapping propensity cost much more accuracy on Chess than on the lookup task, so less skill carried over.

failure_type.evidence: Task difficulty is offered tentatively, but the post says other differences such as longer outputs confound it and no confident conclusion is possible.

quote.value: we observe substantially less capability transfer between propensities
quote.evidence: Summary line saying capability carries over far less across propensity swaps on the most difficult task, the chess puzzles.

audits.notes: Results are in figures; no numeric gaps in text; the performance-gap formula is missing from the extracted text.

audits.title: Function vectors as a model diffing tool: 17 heads repair a bad fine-tune
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a positive result (pasting 17 heads repairs the bad fine-tune) but with detailed negative results: direction injection, a first failed Llama transfer run, and probe-guided layer choice for personas.
experiments: Adding the mean-difference direction to the clean model to install bad medical behavior
Removing that direction from the bad model, which helps but does not cure
First Llama transfer run with a guardrail tuned on Qwen
Probe-peak layers as a guide to where persona traits are load-bearing
Crosscoder search for a feature unique to the bad model
audits.primary_experiment: Adding the mean-difference direction to the clean model to install bad medical behavior

hypothesis.evidence: Cites prior work where one direction works both ways and frames injection as half of a two-way test; no stated expectation of success.

claim_scope.evidence: Layer 15 injection at half the internal-state scale, 15 questions, matched random-direction control, one seed, LoRA bad-medical-advice fine-tunes only; blind LLM judge.

method.evidence: Mean-difference direction between the two models, added to the clean model at scaled doses with random-direction controls; blind LLM judging.

models.evidence: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct bad-medical-advice LoRAs are named; the injection section does not say which one was used.

result_direction.evidence: Injection cut safe answers from 14 to 9 versus 12 under a random direction; just a single additional unsafe answer, despite a big score shift.

failure_type.evidence: Authors judge the direction explains part of the bad behavior yet cannot create it; their frozen-weights account is labeled their own read, not a finding.

quote.value: Adding it to the clean model does almost nothing
quote.evidence: Summary line reporting that injecting the direction into the unbroken model barely changes its behavior.

audits.info_hazard: possible: the failed experiment is an activation-injection attack meant to install unsafe medical behavior; it failed and relies on standard steering, so risk looks low
audits.notes: Mostly a positive repair result; injection test is one section; persona half never names its model; one seed.

audits.title: Sanity Checks for Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders
audits.genuine_reason: Mostly a rebuttal with a positive diagnosis (per-sample normalization fixes BatchTopK), but a long section of failed explanatory hypotheses is described in detail.
experiments: Per-feature loudness added to synthetic activations to explain BatchTopK failure
Raising d_model to 800 and resampling to fix dead latents
Sample-level magnitude variance as the explanation
More true features than latents
Doubling the active feature count to 40
AuxK, hyperparameter sweeps and resampling at d_model 100
audits.primary_experiment: Per-feature loudness added to synthetic activations to explain BatchTopK failure

hypothesis.evidence: Reasoned that different natural loudness per feature might make magnitude a useful signal and improve performance; a footnote calls this motivation poor reasoning.

claim_scope.evidence: Synthetic activations at d_model 800 with 25,600 features and latents, about 20 active features, BatchTopK SAE, loudness drawn from a log-normal with sigma 0.5.

method.evidence: Train BatchTopK SAE on synthetic activations with per-feature loudness multiplier; measure fraction of true features recovered (cosine at least 0.8) and dead latent rate.

models.evidence: BatchTopK SAE trained on synthetic activations; TopK and JumpReLU in related runs; GPT-2 appears only as a source of activation statistics.

result_direction.evidence: BatchTopK recovered 19.6% of features with 78.3% dead latents, worse than the 53.5% baseline at the same size, rather than better.

failure_type.evidence: Author finds loudness by itself fails to account for the difference; a footnote says real SAEs never rely on overall magnitude when picking latents.

quote.value: Instead of improving performance, it actively degrades it
quote.evidence: Says per-feature loudness hurt BatchTopK recovery rather than helping.

audits.notes: Footnote calls the loudness motivation poor; no seeds or error bars reported; the post mainly rebuts a published sanity-check paper.
